content:
# Sirach 31 — Disagreement Log

**Chapter:** SIR 031 | **Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA | **Total Disagreements:** 18

---

## Disagreement 1 — v.1: "wakefulness" vs. "sleeplessness"

- **EMET:** "Wakefulness over wealth wastes away the flesh"
- **LOGOS:** "Sleeplessness over wealth wastes the body"
- **PNEUMA:** "Worrying about wealth can wear a person to the bone"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "Sleeplessness" (LOGOS) — more natural English; PNEUMA's paraphrase loses the physical-spiritual dual meaning of "flesh" (σάρκα).

---

## Disagreement 2 — v.2: "cuts off" vs. "destroys"

- **EMET:** "Wakeful anxiety cuts off slumber"
- **LOGOS:** "Anxious worry cuts off slumber"
- **PNEUMA:** "Restless worry destroys your sleep"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "cuts off" — literal rendering of ἀφαιρεῖ preserves sharpness; PNEUMA's "destroys" is slightly too strong.

---

## Disagreement 3 — v.5: "will not be justified" vs. "cannot be called righteous"

- **EMET:** "He who loves gold will not be justified"
- **LOGOS:** "Whoever loves gold will not be declared righteous"
- **PNEUMA:** "No one who is obsessed with gold can be called righteous"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "will not be justified" — the Greek δικαιωθήσεται carries forensic overtones (justification before God) that PNEUMA loses with "called righteous."

---

## Disagreement 4 — v.9: "call him blessed" vs. "congratulate them"

- **EMET/LOGOS:** "we will call him blessed"
- **PNEUMA:** "We would congratulate them" (with gender-neutral shift)
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "we will call him blessed" — μακαριοῦμεν αὐτόν is the beatitude formula; "congratulate" is too casual and loses the religious register.

---

## Disagreement 5 — v.11: "good things will be made secure" vs. "prosperity will be established"

- **EMET:** "His good things will be made secure"
- **LOGOS:** "His prosperity will be established"
- **PNEUMA:** "Such a person's good fortune will last"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "prosperity will be established" — LOGOS captures both senses (material and moral goods) without EMET's awkward plural.

---

## Disagreement 6 — v.13: "evil eye" interpretation

- **EMET:** "an evil eye is a wicked thing" (preserves Semitic idiom literally)
- **LOGOS:** same
- **PNEUMA:** "a greedy eye is a wicked thing" (interprets the idiom)
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** Preserve "evil eye" as the idiomatic form; the Semitic idiom is widely known enough in English. PNEUMA's gloss is accurate but interpretive.

---

## Disagreement 7 — v.13b: "sheds tears" vs. "weeps"

- **EMET:** "it sheds tears from every face"
- **LOGOS:** "it weeps from every face"
- **PNEUMA:** "that's why it weeps from every face"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "it weeps from every face" — shorter and more natural; the theological point (envy causes suffering in the one who envies) is preserved.

---

## Disagreement 8 — v.15: "Understand what your neighbor feels" vs. "Judge your neighbor's feelings"

- **EMET:** "Understand what your neighbor feels by your own experience"
- **LOGOS:** "Judge your neighbor's feelings by your own"
- **PNEUMA:** "Judge how your neighbor feels by how you would feel in their place"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "Judge your neighbor's feelings by your own experience" — combines EMET's "experience" with LOGOS's "judge."

---

## Disagreement 9 — v.19: "does not gasp" vs. "sleeps soundly"

- **EMET:** "he does not gasp upon his bed"
- **LOGOS:** "He does not pant upon his bed"
- **PNEUMA:** "such a person sleeps soundly"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "does not gasp for breath upon his bed" — preserves the physical vividness that PNEUMA sacrifices.

---

## Disagreement 10 — v.20: "healthy sleep" vs. "sound sleep"

- **EMET:** "Healthy sleep comes from moderate eating"
- **LOGOS:** "Sound sleep comes with a disciplined stomach"
- **PNEUMA:** "Moderation at the table means healthy sleep"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "Sound sleep comes with moderate eating" — LOGOS's adjective, EMET's phrasing.

---

## Disagreement 11 — v.20b: description of glutton's ailments

- **EMET:** "pain of sleeplessness and colic and the torment of the belly"
- **LOGOS:** "agony of sleeplessness, nausea, and gripping pain"
- **PNEUMA:** "insomnia, nausea, and stomach cramps"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "pain of sleeplessness, nausea, and gripping colic" — keeps the three-part structure; "nausea" is clearer than EMET's "colic" alone but more dignified than PNEUMA's "stomach cramps."

---

## Disagreement 12 — v.22: address length

- **EMET:** "Hear me, my child, and do not despise me"
- **LOGOS:** "Listen to me, my child, and do not disregard me"
- **PNEUMA:** "Listen to me, child — don't dismiss what I'm saying"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "Hear me, my child, and do not disregard me" — "Hear me" echoes Ben Sira's characteristic address formula; "disregard" (LOGOS) is better than "despise."

---

## Disagreement 13 — v.23: structure of praise

- **EMET:** "Him who is generous with bread, men will speak well of him"
- **LOGOS:** "The generous man — people will speak well of him"
- **PNEUMA:** "The generous host earns everyone's praise"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "The generous man is spoken well of by everyone" — smooths EMET's awkward construction without PNEUMA's narrowing to "host."

---

## Disagreement 14 — v.24: "grudging with bread" vs. "miser"

- **EMET:** "Him who is grudging with bread"
- **LOGOS:** "The miser"
- **PNEUMA:** "The stingy host"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "The miser" (LOGOS) — single word carries weight; "grudging with bread" is too specific and PNEUMA's "host" is too narrow.

---

## Disagreement 15 — v.25: "show yourself valiant" vs. "try to prove your strength"

- **EMET:** "Do not show yourself valiant in wine"
- **LOGOS:** "Do not put yourself forward in wine-drinking"
- **PNEUMA:** "Don't try to prove your strength by drinking wine"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "Do not show yourself valiant in wine-drinking" — preserves the agonistic warrior metaphor implicit in the Greek; LOGOS is too bland.

---

## Disagreement 16 — v.26: forge metaphor

- **EMET:** "The furnace proves the tempered blade"
- **LOGOS:** "The furnace tests the work of the smith"
- **PNEUMA:** "Fire tests steel in the forge"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "The furnace tests the tempered blade" — EMET's noun "blade" is more specific and poetic than LOGOS's "work of the smith."

---

## Disagreement 17 — v.27: "What is life to a man who is without wine?"

- **EMET/LOGOS/PNEUMA:** All render this as rhetorical question; slight phrasing differences only.
- **LOGOS:** "What life is there for a man who lacks wine?" — most natural.
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** Follows LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 18 — v.31: "distress him by making demands" vs. "press demands"

- **EMET:** "do not distress him by making demands"
- **LOGOS:** "do not press him with demands"
- **PNEUMA:** "don't pester him with demands"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "do not distress him by pressing demands" — combines both; "pester" (PNEUMA) is too informal for the wisdom-literature register.
